title: Human psychology
description: Guess first, then see why a choice can feel right.
author: claude

topic.title: Human psychology
topic.description: Guess first, then see why a choice can feel right.

modules.title: Why we do what we do

concepts.title: Habits
concepts.hook: One missed day did not reset habit growth in Lally's study; the fitted time to near full habit strength ran from 18 to 254 days.
concepts.rule: A cue can start a learned act. Repeating it in a stable setting can strengthen the cue link. In Lally and team’s study, time to near full habit strength varied a lot; one missed day did not wipe it out.

claims.text: Cues in a stable setting can bring back a learned action.
In Lally and team’s study, modeled times ranged from 18 to 254 days; one missed chance did not undo habit growth.

items.stem: Each day after hostel dinner, Nikhil reaches for a notebook on the same desk. What might start the action?

options.text: The familiar dinner-and-desk cue.
options.feedback: The repeated setting can bring back the learned act before he thinks much about a goal.

options.text: Reaching the same number of practice days as everyone else.
options.feedback: Repetition matters, so a fixed day target can sound useful. In this scene, the familiar desk is the cue that starts the action.

items.stem: During exam week, Tara misses one usual evening sketch. What does habit research suggest about that single gap?

options.text: One miss need not erase the learned link.
options.feedback: In the study, an occasional missed chance did not make earlier habit growth vanish.

options.text: The whole habit must return to zero.
options.feedback: One gap can feel like a reset. The learned cue link can still be there the next day.

items.stem: A coach says every habit forms in 21 days. In Lally’s study, people varied widely. About how many days was the median fitted time to near-full automaticity?

options.text: 66 days.
options.feedback: The study’s median was 66 days, while individual fitted times varied from 18 to 254.

options.text: 21 days.
options.feedback: The 21-day rule is easy to recall. The study found a 66-day median and wide spread.

items.stem: A student opens a music app after placing a bag on one hook. What is the likely cue in this example?

options.text: Seeing the bag on that hook.
options.feedback: The repeated place can become linked to the act even when the student's goal changes.

options.text: The student's goal to hear more music.
options.feedback: A goal can motivate app use, but the bag on the hook is the immediate cue that precedes this repeated action.

items.stem: A student keeps the same goal after moving rooms, yet starts a practiced action less often. Why could the move matter?

options.text: The old room’s cue may be absent.
options.feedback: The repeated setting can trigger the action; a new room may not provide that learned cue.

options.text: A strong goal should work just as well in any room.
options.feedback: The goal stays the same, so this feels right. The old cue may be gone.

options.text: The goal alone can recreate the old room cue in any new room.
options.feedback: The goal is still there, but it does not bring back the old room cue on its own.

items.stem: A cue appears, an act follows, and the link grows with repeats. The cue is part of the ___.

options.text: Setting that comes before the act.
options.feedback: Habits join a response to features of its usual context, such as place or prior action.

options.text: Reward promised after every attempt.
options.feedback: A reward can follow an act, so it is easy to mix up. A cue comes first.

items.stem: A student acts by habit after 21 days. A coach says every teammate will do the same by day 21. What is missing?

options.text: People and actions can vary widely.
options.feedback: One person’s timing cannot set a universal deadline; fitted times in the study spanned many weeks.

options.text: The 21-day mark is the same for every action.
options.feedback: One clear number is easy to teach. The study found wide gaps across acts and people.

options.text: Sharing a cue can guarantee every teammate forms the habit by day 21.
options.feedback: A shared cue need not make different people reach the same habit strength on one day.

items.stem: Put this familiar habit loop in a plausible order.

options.text: First: the usual cue appears.
options.feedback: The setting comes before the practiced response in this simple account of a habit.

options.text: Next: the learned response follows.
options.feedback: Repeated pairing can make the action follow the cue with less thought over time.

misconceptions.name: One fixed day count
misconceptions.correction: Habit time varies by person and act; there is no fixed day count.

misconceptions.name: One miss resets all
misconceptions.correction: One missed chance did not wipe out habit growth in the study.

misconceptions.name: Goal replaces cue
misconceptions.correction: A steady goal may not start a habit when a usual cue is gone.

sources.title: How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world
sources.publisher: Lally et al., European Journal of Social Psychology

sources.title: A new look at habits and the habit-goal interface

quest.title: Spot a cue
quest.detail: Watch one harmless daily act. Name the cue, the act, and the good result that may help it recur.

concepts.title: Loss aversion
concepts.hook: In classic choice experiments, the value curve is steeper for losses than for equal gains around a starting point.
concepts.rule: Loss aversion is a pattern where a loss can feel stronger than a same-size gain. It is a tendency in choices, not a law for every person or every case.

claims.text: Prospect theory treats gains and losses relative to a reference point.
Losses can weigh more than equal gains in choice.

items.stem: At a hostel game, Dev has ten tokens and loses one. How might that feel beside gaining one from ten?

options.text: The loss may feel stronger.
options.feedback: Prospect theory models changes from a starting point, with losses often carrying extra weight.

options.text: Equal token size can force both feelings to be exactly equal.
options.feedback: The token amounts match, so equal feelings seem fair. A loss may feel stronger.

items.stem: In a cricket pool, a student is handed ₹50, then asked to risk losing it for a chance at ₹50 more. Which pull may matter?

options.text: The possible loss of the held ₹50.
options.feedback: Once the amount feels owned, giving it up can weigh more than a same-size gain.

options.text: Only the possible gain can matter.
options.feedback: The extra ₹50 draws the eye. Losing the ₹50 already held can also shape the choice.

items.stem: In a toy model of loss aversion, a 10-point loss feels twice as strong as a 10-point gain. About how many gained points would balance that loss in felt value?

options.text: 20 points.
options.feedback: In the stated toy model, a larger gain is needed to match the felt weight of the loss.

options.text: 10 points.
options.feedback: Ten matches the point loss. In this model, that loss feels twice as strong.

items.stem: A student hears the same final score framed as “keep five” or “lose five.” What changed?

options.text: The frame around the starting point.
options.feedback: A reference point can shift how a result is felt even if the arithmetic stays the same.

options.text: The number of points at stake.
options.feedback: The word lose can feel like more is at stake. Both lines still name five points.

items.stem: Two choices have the same final money, but one is framed as a loss from what a person holds. Why might they feel different?

options.text: The starting reference point changes the felt value.
options.feedback: A drop from what is held can weigh more than an equal gain from another starting point.

options.text: Only the size of the final sum shapes the choice.
options.feedback: The end sum looks like the whole story. The starting point can change how it feels.

options.text: Equal final money forces equal felt value.
options.feedback: The end sums match, so equal feelings seem likely. The frame can still change felt value.

items.stem: Prospect theory compares changes with a starting point. A move below it is framed as a ___.

options.text: Loss.
options.feedback: The reference point is key: the same final amount can be viewed through different frames.

options.text: Smaller gain than expected.
options.feedback: Falling below a hoped-for result can feel disappointing, but the model calls a move below the starting point a loss.

items.stem: A study group shows loss aversion on average. A coach predicts exactly twice the pain for every player. What is unsupported?

options.text: A group pattern is not one fixed personal ratio.
options.feedback: People differ. The study shows a common trend, not one set amount for every person.

options.text: The same loss must feel worse to every player.
options.feedback: The group trend is strong, so this sounds safe. It does not set each player's feeling.

options.text: A group average fixes each person’s response.
options.feedback: A group average is easy to reuse. It does not set how each player feels.

items.stem: Match the change to its label from a ten-token start.

options.text: Ten to eleven
options.feedback: Moving above the start adds one token, so it belongs on the gain side.

options.text: A gain of one token
options.feedback: One extra token sits above the start, so its sign is positive in this example.

options.text: Ten to nine
options.feedback: The end count sits below the same start, making this a loss of one token.

options.text: A loss of one token
options.feedback: The number fell by one; its felt weight may still differ from an equal gain.

misconceptions.name: Equal feel
misconceptions.correction: Equal gain and loss can have a different felt weight.

misconceptions.name: Always true
misconceptions.correction: The pattern does not fix how every person will feel.

sources.title: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk

quest.title: Frame a token
quest.detail: Write a made-up choice as a gain and then as a loss from a starting point. Ask how the frame may shift its feel.

concepts.title: Anchoring
concepts.hook: A random number can pull a later estimate: the first figure matters even when it has no link to the answer.
concepts.rule: An early number can pull a later guess toward it. That first number may be useful or random, so the guess needs a check beyond the anchor.

claims.text: A first number can pull a later guess toward it.
An anchor can pull a guess even when the first number is arbitrary.

items.stem: At a family shop, a tag first says ₹900 and then ₹600. What may shape a student's first price guess?

options.text: The ₹900 first number.
options.feedback: An early figure can pull a later judgment before any outside price is checked.

options.text: The ₹900 tag proves ₹600 is a fair price.
options.feedback: The cut looks large. That first tag is set by the seller, not an outside check.

options.text: The later ₹600 price alone, without the old tag.
options.feedback: The current price looks like the obvious clue, but the first ₹900 tag can anchor the guess about what is fair.

items.stem: On a train, two classmates guess the cost of a school trip. One first hears ₹2,000; the other hears ₹8,000. What might differ?

options.text: Their first guesses may be pulled apart.
options.feedback: Each guess can start near the first number heard. The numbers may have been made up.

options.text: The same trip cost can force their first guesses to match.
options.feedback: Both guess the same trip cost, so matching guesses seem likely. Their first numbers differ.

items.stem: In an anchoring study, one group saw a random 65% before guessing a percentage. About what median guess did that high-anchor group give?

options.feedback: The high anchor pulled the group median upward; the low-anchor group’s median was 25%.
The 65% card was vivid, so it is easy to reuse. The group's median guess was 45%.

items.stem: Which clue would test whether a marked-down pen is cheap?

options.text: A price for the same pen elsewhere.
options.feedback: A second shop's price gives a fresh clue that the first tag cannot give.

options.text: The crossed-out number alone.
options.feedback: The old tag looks like a bargain clue. The seller may have set it high.

items.stem: A school quiz shows a random 65 before asking for a percentage. Why might guesses still shift after students hear that it is random?

options.text: They may adjust from the first number.
options.feedback: The first number can pull later guesses, even when it gives no real clue.

options.text: Knowing the number is random stops it from shaping a guess.
options.feedback: The warning should help. Yet people can still start near the first number they saw.

options.text: A random number can serve as a valid sample of the real answer.
options.feedback: It appeared right before the question, so it can feel relevant. The number was random.

items.stem: A student guesses near a figure printed on a poster, then adjusts a little. That first figure is an ___.

options.text: Anchor.
options.feedback: The first number can tug a guess, even if the poster gives no real clue.

options.text: Independent check.
options.feedback: A printed figure looks official. It is the first cue, not an outside check.

items.stem: A seller crosses out ₹500 and asks ₹300. A buyer treats the old tag as independent proof of fair value. What is the flaw?

options.text: The seller may control that first number.
options.feedback: The crossed-out tag can anchor a guess without measuring the item’s value elsewhere.

options.text: A large marked-down amount proves a good deal.
options.feedback: The cut price catches the eye. A price from another seller is a better check.

options.text: The old price tag can prove fair value without an outside check.
options.feedback: Two tags look like two prices. Both came from the same seller, so neither is an outside check.

items.stem: Which line best sums up anchoring in a quiz?

options.text: An early number can tug a later guess.
options.feedback: Even a made-up first number can pull a later guess toward it.

options.text: The latest number can erase the effect of an earlier one.
options.feedback: The latest number feels fresh. The first one can still tug the later guess.

misconceptions.name: First means fair
misconceptions.correction: The first number is not proof of the fair value.

misconceptions.name: Random has no pull
misconceptions.correction: Even an arbitrary first number can sway a later guess.

sources.title: Problem Solving, Psychology 2e
Overcoming Cognitive Biases and Engaging in Critical Reflection
Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases

quest.title: Compare tags
quest.detail: Pick two made-up price tags. Start a guess from each, then see how the first number may pull the guess.

concepts.title: Confirmation bias
concepts.hook: In Wason's rule task, many people picked a card that could confirm the rule and skipped one that could break it.
concepts.rule: Confirmation bias is a pull to seek or notice clues that fit a belief. A fair test also looks for clues that could show the belief is wrong.

claims.text: People can focus on clues that fit a prior belief while missing other clues.
A test of an idea is stronger when it can find a case that goes against it.

items.stem: In exam week, Aditi thinks every hard paper hides a trick question. Which memory of hers shows this bias at work?

options.text: The one with a trick question.
options.feedback: A matching case fits her belief and may stand out more than a plain paper.

options.text: A paper with no trick question.
options.feedback: A paper with no trick is easy to set aside. It could test her claim that all have one.

items.stem: A family shop owner thinks rain always cuts sales. What record would test the claim best?

options.text: Days with rain and steady sales too.
options.feedback: A possible exception can show whether the word “always” holds up across the records.

options.text: Only the wettest low-sales day.
options.feedback: A wet slow day fits her view. Rainy days with steady sales could test it better.

items.stem: In a Wason-style test, a rule could be checked by seeking a disconfirming card. About what percent in one nonthreatening-rule group chose the correct card pair?

options.feedback: Only a small share chose both cards needed to test the rule for a possible counterexample.
The large share left over seems close. Only 16% chose the key pair.

items.stem: A cricket fan says a batter always flops in chases. Which scorecard matters most for checking “always”?

options.text: A successful chase innings.
options.feedback: One clear counterexample is enough to break a claim with the word “always.”

options.text: Another poor chase innings.
options.feedback: A poor chase fits the fan's view. One good chase could break the word always.

items.stem: A rule predicts that every late bus is red. Why is checking a late bus that is not red useful?

options.text: It could disprove the universal rule.
options.feedback: A red late bus fits the rule, but one late bus of another colour would break it.

options.text: A late red bus confirms the rule for all buses.
options.feedback: A match feels like proof. One late bus of another colour would break the rule.

options.text: More red buses can outweigh one late bus of another colour.
options.feedback: A single late bus of another colour would break the rule, no matter how many red matches were found.

items.stem: A student saves only screenshots that support her guess. She is filtering evidence toward ___.

options.text: Her existing belief.
options.feedback: The pattern can make a weak idea seem stronger by hiding cases that point away.

options.text: A well-tested belief, because she found matching examples.
options.feedback: A few matches can feel like proof. Yet the skipped cases may show the guess is wrong.

items.stem: A student saves three bus logs that fit her belief and skips two that do not. She calls the belief proven. What is the flaw?

options.text: The saved sample leaves out contrary cases.
options.feedback: Selecting only matches can make a weak belief look stronger than the full record supports.

options.text: Only the saved matches count as evidence.
options.feedback: Saved cases feel clear and close at hand. The skipped logs can test the belief too.

options.text: Three saved logs outweigh every omitted log.
options.feedback: Three saved matches look strong. The skipped logs may be the cases that break the claim.

items.stem: How can a student miss clues against a belief?

options.text: We may notice support and miss possible exceptions.
options.feedback: The bias lies in uneven search or recall, regardless of whether the starting idea is true.

options.text: A strong belief can make every clue equally easy to remember.
options.feedback: Memory can feel fair. Yet we may recall what fits our view and miss what does not.

misconceptions.name: One match proves it
misconceptions.correction: One fitting case may fit more than one idea.

misconceptions.name: Disproof is useless
misconceptions.correction: A case against an idea can test it well.

sources.title: Problem Solving, Psychology 2e
Motivated Reasoning and Performance on the Wason Selection Task
sources.publisher: Dawson, Gilovich and Regan, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

quest.title: Try to disprove
quest.detail: Pick a low-stakes belief about a game or bus. Write one clue that could show it is wrong.

concepts.title: Social proof
concepts.hook: In Asch's line task, a plainly wrong group answer still pulled some participants away from what they saw.
concepts.rule: A crowd choice can act as a clue and pull a person’s choice. But a crowd can be wrong; group agreement is not proof.

claims.text: In Asch’s line task, group answers sometimes pulled a person toward a wrong answer.
Group agreement is social input, not proof that a claim is true.

items.stem: At a hostel quiz, most students pick the wrong line length aloud. What may happen to the last student's answer?

options.text: It may move toward the group choice.
options.feedback: A public majority can change some answers even when the visual task seems clear.

options.text: A clear line task can keep every answer fully independent.
options.feedback: The line looks clear, so a solo choice seems safe. Some people still followed the wrong group.

items.stem: During a cricket watch party, everyone cheers a disputed call before the replay. What might the crowd signal do?

options.text: Make the call seem more certain.
options.feedback: The cheers come first. They can sway a guess before the replay gives a clear view.

options.text: Prove the call was right.
options.feedback: The crowd sounds sure, so the call may feel settled. The replay can still show it was wrong.

items.stem: In Asch’s line task, a group gave wrong answers aloud. About what percent of critical answers from the lone participant followed the wrong group?

options.text: About 37%.
options.feedback: Asch reported 36.8% wrong answers on critical trials, showing a strong group pull.

options.text: About 1%.
options.feedback: One percent sounds right for an easy line task. The wrong group pulled far more answers.

items.stem: A whole class picks the same answer to an easy line puzzle. What does that show by itself?

options.text: Agreement, not proof of accuracy.
options.feedback: The group may share a mistake, so a headcount alone cannot settle the visual fact.

options.text: The answer is certainly right.
options.feedback: A full class can look like proof. They may share the same wrong cue.

items.stem: A student sees a clear line match but publicly follows a wrong group answer. Why can this happen?

options.text: Fitting in can outweigh a private judgment.
options.feedback: In Asch’s task, public group pressure could pull answers away from the visible line lengths.

options.text: A clear line match cannot be swayed by public votes.
options.feedback: The lines look clear, so this sounds likely. Group pressure can still shift a public answer.

options.text: The group’s vote can show that her clear visual check was wrong.
options.feedback: A unanimous group can seem more reliable than one person's view, but its votes can sway a public answer without changing the lines.

items.stem: If a crowd's visible choice nudges a person's own choice, the crowd is serving as a ___.

options.text: Social cue.
options.feedback: The signal comes from what others did, though its size does not make it reliable.

options.text: Private measurement.
options.feedback: Many votes look like many checks. The votes can sway one another.

items.stem: A group chooses B before anyone checks the evidence. A student calls their unanimous votes independent proof. What is missing?

options.text: Their votes may influence one another.
options.feedback: A shared answer can spread through a group, so agreement alone is not a fresh check.

options.text: More votes make a wrong choice true.
options.feedback: A crowd can feel like strong proof. Its size does not fix a wrong answer.

options.text: Unanimous votes can guarantee independent checks.
options.feedback: All votes match, so they look independent. The first answer may have shaped the rest.

items.stem: Which explanation fits the line-length result in Asch's task?

options.text: A wrong majority sometimes shifted individual answers.
options.feedback: The finding shows influence in that setting, while people did not all copy every time.

options.text: Every participant copied on every trial.
options.feedback: A strong group pull sounds like it works every time. Some people kept their own answer.

misconceptions.name: Crowd proves truth
misconceptions.correction: A group can agree on a wrong answer.

misconceptions.name: No one is swayed
misconceptions.correction: Group answers can pull some people in some settings.

sources.title: Conformity, Compliance, and Obedience, Psychology 2e
Opinions and Social Pressure

quest.title: Watch a group cue
quest.detail: In a harmless choice, note whether a visible group choice changes a guess. Keep the check kind.

concepts.title: The planning fallacy
concepts.hook: In a study, students thought their papers would take less time than they did. Even their best guesses ran short.
concepts.rule: The planning fallacy is a tilt toward a short time guess for our own task. Looking at past tasks and missed steps can give a better time guess.

claims.text: People can underguess how long their own tasks will take.
Plans can miss delays that happened in similar past work.

items.stem: A hostel team says its chart will take one hour but has not counted printing. What might happen?

options.text: It may take longer than guessed.
options.feedback: Missing a step from the imagined path can make the finish time estimate too short.

options.text: Printing time does not count as project work.
options.feedback: The chart may be done in an hour. It still takes time to print and finish.

options.text: The one-hour target can include printing without adding any time.
options.feedback: One hour is the team's clear target. It still leaves out print work.

items.stem: During exam week, Isha plans a revision sheet and forgets to gather past papers. Which estimate is at risk?

options.text: Her own finish-time guess.
options.feedback: The missing collection step adds work outside the smooth path she pictured.

options.text: Only the time spent writing the revision sheet.
options.feedback: Writing feels like the main task, but collecting papers is another step and can make the whole plan take longer.

items.stem: A club plans posters in 2 hours but forgot printing. Similar past posters took 3, 4, and 5 hours. About how many hours does the past-task view suggest?

options.text: 4 hours.
options.feedback: Past completed jobs give a four-hour comparison point that includes steps the new plan missed.

options.text: 2 hours.
options.feedback: Two hours is the team's own guess. Past posters took three to five hours.

items.stem: A student plans only the time to draw a poster. What other work needs time?

options.text: Time to find and print the images.
options.feedback: Finding and printing images take time beyond the drawing step she counted.

options.text: The drawing time already counted.
options.feedback: Counting the same drawing time again does not cover the tasks she left out.

items.stem: A team imagines a smooth poster project and ignores likely printing delays. Why can its time guess run short?

options.text: The plan leaves out a common work step.
options.feedback: The imagined best case omits printing time that similar real tasks may include.

options.text: The missing print step is too small to affect the guess.
options.feedback: It can look like a quick last step. Past tasks show such work still takes time.

options.text: A smooth plan makes unlisted steps take no time.
options.feedback: The planned parts may go well. The print step still takes time even then.

items.stem: To compare a new task with old ones, the useful number is the time those old tasks ___.

options.text: Actually took.
options.feedback: Old jobs show the time used, with snags and steps the new plan may miss.

options.text: Were first hoped to take.
options.feedback: Old plans are easy to compare. Old finish times show what the work took.

items.stem: Past posters took four to six hours. A new plan says one hour because artwork is ready, but printing is uncounted. What is weak?

options.text: The guess omits a step and dismisses past times.
options.feedback: Ready artwork may help, yet the past tasks and missing printing step still matter.

options.text: The new plan makes the past times useless.
options.feedback: The ready art is a real change. Yet past times can still flag missed tasks such as print.

options.text: Ready artwork proves all other steps vanish.
options.feedback: Ready art does save time. It does not make print and other steps vanish.

items.stem: Which sentence sums up the planning fallacy in a school project?

options.text: A smooth imagined path can understate real time.
options.feedback: Past completed jobs can reveal delays that a new plan has not pictured.

options.text: Every late job can be explained by a poor initial estimate.
options.feedback: A late job can look like a bad plan. This idea is about time guesses, not every delay.

misconceptions.name: Best case is normal
misconceptions.correction: A smooth plan is only one path; delays can add time.

misconceptions.name: Past tasks do not help
misconceptions.correction: Past task times can show steps a new plan has missed.

sources.title: Exploring the Planning Fallacy: Why People Underestimate Their Task Completion Times
sources.publisher: Buehler, Griffin and Ross, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

quest.title: Time a small task
quest.detail: Before a small school task, note a time guess. Afterward, note the time and one step the guess missed.

concepts.title: Sleep and memory
concepts.hook: New learning can become more stable during sleep, even without another round of practice.
concepts.rule: Sleep supports the later strengthening and organising of some new memories; it does not replace learning in the first place.

claims.text: Studies find that sleep after learning can help later recall.
Sleep can help new memories in many tasks. Quiet rest can help too.

items.stem: After a hostel student learns a short poem, a night of sleep follows. What can happen to the new memory?

options.text: It may become more stable.
options.feedback: In some tests, sleep after study helps people recall more later.

options.text: Sleep can only pause learning; it cannot help keep the poem.
options.feedback: No new lines are practiced during sleep, so it can seem idle. Sleep can help stabilise what was learned earlier.

items.stem: During exam week, Rohan reads a chapter once, then sleeps. Which part is the initial learning?

options.text: Reading the chapter.
options.feedback: The material first has to be encoded before later processing can help keep it.

options.text: The night of sleep after reading.
options.feedback: Sleep can help keep what was read. But the first step was to read it.

items.stem: In a small word-pair study, average recall after 12 hours was 20.38 pairs with sleep and 12.63 after wakefulness. About what percent higher was recall after sleep?

options.text: About 60% higher.
options.feedback: The difference is 7.75 pairs. Divide by the wake score, 12.63, to get about 61%. This was one small study.

options.text: About 38% higher.
options.feedback: Dividing 7.75 by the sleep score uses the larger group as the base. Compared with wake recall, the gain was about 61%.

options.text: About the same.
options.feedback: Both groups learned pairs, but after 12 hours this study found higher recall after sleep.

items.stem: A student learns a poem, then recalls it better the next day. What could help the memory last?

options.text: Consolidation after the first lesson.
options.feedback: After the first lesson, the brain can help keep the new memory over time.

options.text: The first reading of the poem.
options.feedback: Reading starts the trace. The question asks what can strengthen it after that first encounter.

items.stem: A student sleeps after practice and recalls a skill better. Why is sleep a plausible part of the story?

options.text: Some new traces are processed after practice.
options.feedback: Sleep can aid recall. One test alone does not show each brain step.

options.text: Sleep alone can teach the skill with no practice.
options.feedback: Better recall after sleep can look like new learning. The skill was first learned during practice.

options.text: Practice alone explains the gain; sleep played no part.
options.feedback: Practice came first, so it is easy to credit it all. Sleep may also help keep a new skill.

items.stem: First a student learns a word; later the memory becomes steadier. The later step is ___.

options.text: Consolidation.
options.feedback: It names changes after initial learning that can help the word remain available.

options.text: The first encounter.
options.feedback: The first sight of the word matters. The gap asks for what helps keep it later.

items.stem: A classmate says no memory can strengthen while someone is awake. What is too broad?

options.text: Quiet waking rest can also help.
options.feedback: Sleep has an important role, but studies also find gains after low-interference rest.

options.text: Quiet rest does nothing because the person stays awake.
options.feedback: Sleep has a known role, so this seems likely. Waking rest can help as well.

options.text: Only sleep can change a memory.
options.feedback: Sleep gets more notice in memory studies. Quiet rest can also help new learning last.

items.stem: Which line best sums up sleep and new learning?

options.text: Sleep can help keep what was learned.
options.feedback: It can help keep what was learned. It does not teach new facts alone.

options.text: Sleep can create knowledge of a chapter that was never read.
options.feedback: Sleep can help after study, so it may sound like a teacher. The chapter must be read first.

misconceptions.name: Sleep is only a pause
misconceptions.correction: The brain can process recent learning during sleep.

misconceptions.name: Sleep teaches unseen material
misconceptions.correction: Sleep can help store what was learned, but it does not supply an unread lesson.

Memory Consolidation during Waking Rest
Sleep-dependent memory consolidation and accelerated forgetting

quest.title: Trace a lesson
quest.detail: In a made-up study day, mark learning first and later memory processing.

concepts.title: Variable rewards
concepts.hook: An unpredictable good post can make the next swipe tempting even after several dull ones.
concepts.rule: When rewards arrive at uneven times, the next try can seem worth checking. This can help explain repeated feed use.

claims.text: A reward now and then can draw more checks in some cases.
A study found that likes can shape posts. It did not test one set rule for each feed.

items.stem: At a hostel, a student scrolls past dull posts, then finds a funny one. What might draw another swipe?

options.text: The next good post is uncertain.
options.feedback: A fun find now and then can make the next swipe feel worth it.

options.text: Every next post is certain to be funny.
options.feedback: The last post was fun, so another feels likely. The next one can still be dull.

items.stem: During a train ride, likes arrive at uneven times on a college post. Why might the app be checked again?

options.text: The next social reward is hard to predict.
options.feedback: Research found that social feedback can shape when people return to post or check.

options.text: Likes must arrive at set time gaps after posting.
options.feedback: A steady clock would be easy to predict. Likes in the case arrive at uneven times.

options.text: A fixed reward appears after every check.
options.feedback: A new check can feel due for a like. Likes can arrive at uneven times.

items.stem: In a toy feed with variable rewards, each swipe has an independent 20% chance of a fun clip. After five swipes, about what is the chance of seeing at least one fun clip?

options.text: About 67%.
options.feedback: The chance of no clip is 0.8 to the fifth power, about 33%. So at least one is about 67%, with no guarantee.

options.text: 100%, because one in five means a clip by swipe five.
options.feedback: One in five is a chance on each swipe, not a promise every fifth swipe. Five misses are still possible.

options.text: 20%, the same as one swipe.
options.feedback: Each swipe has a 20% chance, but five independent chances raise the chance of at least one clip to about 67%.

items.stem: What does variable mean in a reward pattern?

options.text: The timing or count can change.
options.feedback: The next payoff does not arrive after one fixed number of actions.

options.text: A variable schedule can guarantee a payoff after every action.
options.feedback: A good clip may follow a swipe. It does not follow each one.

items.stem: A friend says feeds use precisely the same schedule as every slot machine. Why is that too exact?

options.text: Feeds and users can differ.
options.feedback: The link is the unsure payoff. Feeds do not all have one set rule.

options.text: A feed must reward every set number of swipes.
options.feedback: A slot machine can suggest a strict rule. Feed posts and likes can vary in other ways.

options.text: Feeds can only reward all users on one fixed swipe count.
options.feedback: The slot machine link invites one clock. Feeds and users can have different patterns.

items.stem: A reward comes after some checks, but not after each one. The pattern is ___.

options.text: Intermittent.
options.feedback: Some actions bring a rewarding result while others do not.

options.text: Guaranteed on every check.
options.feedback: Past checks can bring a reward, so a sure next one sounds fair. The gap can vary.

items.stem: A classmate says uncertain rewards alone explain why anyone opens a feed. What is missing?

options.text: People can have other motives too.
options.feedback: People can also look for friends, news or a break.

options.text: Each user opens a feed for the same reason.
options.feedback: A shared app can make motives look alike. People may check news, friends, or other things.

options.text: Uncertain rewards can be the only reason anyone opens a feed.
options.feedback: A reward can pull another check. People also open feeds for news or friends.

items.stem: Which line best captures the slot-machine comparison?

options.text: An uncertain payoff can invite another try.
options.feedback: The next nice post is hard to guess. That is the useful link.

options.text: Each swipe can be counted on to pay out on schedule.
options.feedback: A machine can pay on a schedule. This comparison is about not knowing when a good result comes.

misconceptions.name: Every swipe rewards
misconceptions.correction: A good result can come after dull ones, with no set gap.

misconceptions.name: One cause explains all use
misconceptions.correction: People open feeds for many reasons, not just uncertain rewards.

sources.title: Learning lesson plan: reinforcement schedules
A computational reward learning account of social media engagement
Addictive Features of Social Media and Messenger Platforms
sources.publisher: Montag et al., International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health

quest.title: Spot a pattern
quest.detail: Compare a made-up fixed reward sequence with an uneven one.

concepts.title: If-then plans
concepts.hook: A plan tied to a clear moment can help turn a goal into an action.
concepts.rule: An if-then plan names a cue and the action to take when it appears. This link can help people start.

claims.text: An if-then plan links a clear cue to a chosen act.
Studies find that such plans can help goal pursuit compared with a goal alone.

items.stem: A hostel student says, “If dinner ends, then I will open my notes.” What may help start the task?

options.text: Dinner ending acts as a cue.
options.feedback: The plan links a visible moment to the first action, making it easier to notice.

options.text: Writing that sentence makes revision certain after dinner.
options.feedback: The cue is clear, so action may be more likely. A plan cannot make it certain.

options.text: The goal has no moment attached.
options.feedback: Dinner may seem like just a goal. The word if makes its end the start cue.

items.stem: Before a college quiz, Mira says only, “I will revise more.” What is missing from an if-then plan?

options.text: A specific cue and response.
options.feedback: The wish names a goal but no moment that starts a chosen action.

options.text: A larger wish alone.
options.feedback: A bigger wish can feel more firm. It still gives no clear moment to act.

items.stem: A review of 94 tests compared if-then plans with no such plan. About how large was the average gain in goal attainment, measured as Cohen's d?

options.text: About 0.65 standard deviations.
options.feedback: Gollwitzer and Sheeran reported d = 0.65 across 94 tests. It is a standardised effect, not a 65% success rate.

options.text: About 65 percentage points.
options.feedback: The 0.65 figure uses spread in scores as its unit. It does not mean 65 percentage points.

options.text: About zero; plans showed no average effect.
options.feedback: A bare goal may not trigger action. Across these tests, specifying a cue and action had a positive average effect.

items.stem: A student plans, “If I sit at my desk, then I draw.” What should tell her when to start?

options.text: Sitting down at the desk.
options.feedback: The desk moment is the cue linked in advance to the drawing action.

options.text: Finishing the drawing first.
options.feedback: Drawing is the response to start when the desk cue appears, not the starting cue itself.

items.stem: A student writes “if I am free, I will study,” but free time is hard to notice. Why may that weaken the plan?

options.text: The cue is vague.
options.feedback: A cue that is hard to spot may not prompt the action at a clear moment.

options.text: A broad cue works as well as a clear event.
options.feedback: Both sound like plans. A clear event is easier to spot when it is time to act.

options.text: All if-then plans work equally well.
options.feedback: Both plans use if and then. A vague cue can still be hard to spot.

items.stem: In an if-then plan, the “then” part names the ___.

options.text: Action to take.
options.feedback: It states the response linked in advance to the selected situation.

options.text: Earlier cue.
options.feedback: The cue comes first, so it is easy to name. The then part names what to do.

items.stem: A coach says an if-then plan makes action certain. What is too strong?

options.text: It helps, but cannot promise every action.
options.feedback: The plans can help on average. They do not make each act sure.

options.text: Writing the plan makes its cue impossible to miss.
options.feedback: A written cue is easier to recall. Busy days can still hide or change it.

options.text: A written plan controls every future event.
options.feedback: Writing a plan can make it feel firm. A cue may still be missed or changed.

items.stem: Which line tells a friend what an if-then plan does?

options.text: It links a named moment with a chosen act.
options.feedback: The cue comes first; the response is ready if that moment arrives.

options.text: It only repeats a large goal.
options.feedback: Both name a goal, so they sound alike. This plan also names a cue and an act.

misconceptions.name: A wish is a plan
misconceptions.correction: A broad goal leaves the moment of action unspecified.

misconceptions.name: A plan guarantees action
misconceptions.correction: Even a specific cue-action link can be missed or changed.

sources.publisher: Gollwitzer and Oettingen, University of Konstanz

Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta-analysis of Effects and Processes
sources.publisher: Gollwitzer and Sheeran, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology

concepts.title: The spotlight effect
concepts.hook: A small slip can feel huge to us. Others may notice it less.
concepts.rule: The spotlight effect means we may guess too many people took note. Some still do.

claims.text: In a shirt test, wearers guessed too many people took note.
In a group talk, speakers thought their words stood out more than they did.

items.stem: A student wears a bright shirt to a college class and expects all classmates to recall it. What might be overestimated?

options.text: How many people noticed the shirt.
options.feedback: In the test, the wearers guessed too high. Fewer people knew the shirt image.

options.text: How bright the fabric looks under light.
options.feedback: A bright shirt catches her own eye. The effect asks how many others took note.

items.stem: At a cricket club talk, Asha slips on one word. She thinks all recall it. What may be happening?

options.text: She may overrate how prominent it was.
options.feedback: In a group talk, speakers guessed their words stood out more than they did.

options.text: All the listeners must recall her slip.
options.feedback: The slip stands out to Asha. Other listeners may have paid it little mind.

options.text: No listener could have noticed the slip.
options.feedback: It may not stand out to most people. Yet some listeners can still catch it.

items.stem: In one shirt test, wearers thought 46% of people would name the image. About what percent in fact did?

options.text: About 23%.
options.feedback: Only about half as many people named the image as the wearers had guessed.

options.text: About 46%.
options.feedback: The 46% guess is easy to recall. Only about 23% of others named the image.

items.stem: What does the spotlight effect describe?

options.text: Overrating how much others notice us.
options.feedback: Our own experience is vivid, so it can loom larger than it does to observers.

options.text: The feeling that everyone noticed is proof that they did.
options.feedback: The mistake feels vivid from the inside, but that feeling can overstate how much others noticed.

items.stem: Why might a small mistake seem huge to the person who made it?

options.text: They know every detail of their own moment.
options.feedback: That vivid inside view can anchor a guess about how much others saw.

options.text: A public slip must stand out as much to others.
options.feedback: The maker felt every detail. Others may have been busy with their own thoughts.

options.text: Others have the same inside view.
options.feedback: The slip filled the maker's mind. Others may have had many other things to watch.

items.stem: The spotlight effect is about a guess of other people’s ___.

options.text: Attention.
options.feedback: The bias is in estimating how much of our action or appearance others notice.

options.text: Judgment of how serious a mistake was.
options.feedback: The slip may feel big to her. This effect asks how many others took note.

items.stem: A friend says the spotlight effect proves nobody notices a public mistake. What is wrong?

options.text: It predicts overestimation, not zero notice.
options.feedback: Some observers may notice; the key is that the person often guesses too many.

options.text: The effect proves the guess is always too high.
options.feedback: The group trend can sound like a fixed law. Any one guess may still be right.

options.text: Every observer always misses it.
options.feedback: People often notice less than we fear. Some can still spot the mistake.

items.stem: Which sentence fairly states the spotlight effect?

options.text: My own moment may feel bigger to me than to others.
options.feedback: The research concerns a gap between my guess and what observers recall.

options.text: Others can be expected to think about me all day.
options.feedback: The moment looms large to us. Others may give it far less thought.

misconceptions.name: Everyone noticed
misconceptions.correction: Our own vivid view can make an event seem more visible to others than it was.

misconceptions.name: Nobody ever notices
misconceptions.correction: Some people may take note. The guess is often too high.

sources.publisher: Gilovich, Medvec and Savitsky, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
